passage:
Coach's note, under-11 football, Saturday. Francis sir.
Before today's final, I asked each boy to write his predicted score on the whiteboard. Samir wrote "We win 3–1" in big letters and drew a trophy. We lost 0–2. In the van home, Samir told the others, "I knew we'd lose. Their goalkeeper was too tall. It was obvious from the start." When Farhan pointed out his whiteboard prediction, Samir said he had "secretly known." He seemed to truly believe it.
What I did: I took a photo of the whiteboard. Next week I'll show it at practice, not to shame anyone, but to talk about how our memory changes after a match.

qa.q: What did Samir write on the whiteboard before the final?
qa.a: Samir wrote "We win 3–1" in big letters and drew a trophy.

qa.q: Why does Samir seem to truly believe he knew they would lose?
qa.a: Once he knew the result, the tall goalkeeper seemed like an obvious clue, and his mind quietly replaced his hopeful prediction with a neater story.

qa.q: Why is the whiteboard photo a good tool for next week?
qa.a: It shows what the boys actually expected before the match, so they can compare it with what they say now and notice how memory rewrites things, without anyone being shamed.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when Samir says he secretly knew?
qa.a: Farhan may feel puzzled or annoyed, since he saw the trophy drawing and knows Samir expected to win.

grounding: Shows a boy claiming after a loss that he knew his team would lose, although he had predicted a win.

passage:
Sunday
Our colony team lost the gully cricket final to C-block today. I knew it all along. Their bowler was too fast and our captain kept dropping catches. Anyone could see it. Alka said, "But yesterday you bet me five toffees we'd win by fifty runs!" That was different. I was just being nice to the team. Jasleen said I made a poster that said CHAMPIONS. That was for fun. Deep inside I always knew. Mummy laughed and called me her know-it-all boy. I don't think it's funny. I'm going to write my prediction for next week here, so nobody can argue.
Jatin

qa.q: How many toffees did Jatin bet Alka?
qa.a: Jatin bet Alka five toffees.

qa.q: Why does Jatin say he was just being nice to the team about the bet?
qa.a: Jatin feels embarrassed about the bet and the poster now that the result is known, and losing seems obvious. So he explains them away to keep the story that he always knew.

qa.q: What could help Jatin see what he really expected before a match?
qa.a: Writing his prediction down before each match, as he plans to, and reading it afterwards will show him what he truly thought at the time.

qa.q: How might Alka feel about Jatin's claim that he knew it all along?
qa.a: Alka may find it funny or annoying, since the five-toffee bet on a big win is still fresh in memory. 😅

grounding: Shows a boy insisting after the match that he knew his team would lose, rewriting his earlier bet and poster.

passage: At the temple fair in their village near Hubballi, the big kabaddi match ended just before sunset. The home team, which Yash had cheered for all afternoon, lost by two points. Walking home along the canal with his sister Rashmi, Yash kicked a pebble. "I knew they'd lose. Their raider was slow. I could tell from the first minute." Rashmi raised an eyebrow. "At half-time you said they'd win easily. You even bet your balloon." "I didn't mean it." "You shouted it." Yash walked faster. "It was obvious," he insisted, "if you watched properly." Behind them, the loudspeakers were already announcing next year's fair.

qa.q: By how many points did the home team lose?
qa.a: The home team lost by two points.

qa.q: Why does the loss seem obvious to Yash now?
qa.a: Yash feels embarrassed by the loss and his bet, so knowing the result makes the slow raider look like a clear sign and his half-time confidence gets rewritten into a story where he always knew.

qa.q: What could Rashmi suggest before next year's match?
qa.a: She could suggest they both say their predictions out loud or write them down before the match and check them afterwards, so they can see what they really expected.

qa.q: What is it like for Rashmi to hear Yash's claim?
qa.a: Rashmi finds it hard to accept, since she clearly remembers him shouting at half-time that they'd win and betting his balloon.

grounding: Shows a boy saying after the match that he knew his team would lose, though at half-time he was sure they would win.

passage: The Osaka school relay ended with the red team crossing first. Hiroshi, nine, had spent the race gripping the rope, shouting for white, his team. "Come on, come on!" Afterwards, eating onigiri on the grass with his sister Noa, he said, "I knew we'd lose. Our third runner is slow. It was obvious." Noa raised an eyebrow. "This morning you said white would win by miles. You bet me your dessert." "No, I didn't. I said it might be close." "You said 'by miles.' Twice." Hiroshi looked at his onigiri. "Well… I sort of knew." Noa laughed. "You knew after it happened." Hiroshi frowned, trying to remember what he really thought that morning. Now the loss seemed certain too. He handed her the dessert anyway.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi bet Noa?
qa.a: His dessert.

qa.q: Why does Hiroshi now feel he knew his team would lose?
qa.a: After the race, the slow third runner seems like an obvious reason, so his mind rewrites the morning's hope into a prediction of losing. Now the loss feels like it was always certain.

qa.q: What could Hiroshi do before the next race to see what he really expected?
qa.a: He could write down his prediction before the race, so afterwards he can check what he actually thought instead of relying on memory.

qa.q: How might Noa see Hiroshi's claim that he knew all along?
qa.a: She finds it funny, since she clearly remembers him saying "by miles" twice, and gently points out that he only knew after it happened.

grounding: A boy says he knew his team would lose the relay, though that morning he had bet they would win easily.

passage: In the boys' hostel common room, twenty children crowded round the TV for the badminton final. Chaitanya, eleven, was loudly sure: "Green shirt will win. He's the champion. No chance for the other one." In the third game, the younger player in blue won every long rally. When blue won the final point, the room exploded. Chaitanya folded his arms. "I knew it. Green was getting tired from the first game. Anyone could see." Lalit sir, the warden, stacked chairs. "Chaitanya, what did you say at the start?" "I said… green might be tired." "I heard 'no chance for the other one.'" A few boys laughed. Chaitanya went pink. "It felt like I knew," he said quietly. Lalit sir nodded. "It always does, afterwards."

qa.q: Who won the final point?
qa.a: The younger player in blue.

qa.q: Why does Chaitanya feel he knew green would lose?
qa.a: Once the match ended, the signs of green getting tired seemed obvious, so his memory changed his confident prediction into "I knew it." It genuinely feels true to him.

qa.q: How could Chaitanya check his memory next time he feels he "knew it all along"?
qa.a: He could say his prediction out loud or write it down before the match, then compare it honestly with the result.

qa.q: How might Lalit sir feel when Chaitanya says "It felt like I knew"?
qa.a: He probably feels kind towards him, glad Chaitanya noticed the trick his memory played, and his reply shows it happens to everyone.

grounding: A boy watching a badminton final claims he knew the champion would lose, though he had said the opposite at the start.
